1.pericope_label: There was a certain man in Cesarea called Cornelius, a centurion of the band called the Italian band, A devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway. He saw in a vision evidently about the ninth hour of the day an angel of God coming in to him, and saying unto him, Cornelius. And when he looked on him, he was afraid, and said, What is it, Lord? And he said unto him, Thy prayers and thine alms are come up for a memorial before God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin cover the identification and the safeguards. Gill fixes the place, the Caesarea formerly called Strato’s tower and not Caesarea Philippi, since the former lay near Joppa; describes Cornelius as truly religious, having forsaken the Roman idolatry and superstition in which he was brought up; insists the vision found him neither dreaming nor in a trance but thoroughly awake with his eyes open in clear day; and accounts for his fear by the brightness of the clothing, the lustre of the countenance and the majestic form, noting that such fear was usual even with good persons — the patriarchs and prophets, Zacharias, the Virgin Mary — from a sense of the greatness of the divine majesty. Calvin calls the history memorable because God advances a stranger and an uncircumcised man to singular honour above all the Jews, sending an angel to him and bringing Peter to Caesarea for his sake. He arranges the virtues by the two tables of the law: Cornelius was godly and feared God; like a good householder he took care to instruct his family; he is praised for the offices of love as beneficent toward all the people; and he prayed to God continually — a man of singular virtues, his life framed in all points to the rule God prescribes. On the vision he treats the stated hour as a deliberate safeguard, since men are often deceived by juggling and Luke records the time to avoid all suspicion, the day being divided into twelve hours so that this was fair daylight and the vision the more evident.

Henry treats the whole episode as a mystery that must be watched closely. The bringing of the gospel to the Gentiles, and the bringing of those who had been strangers and foreigners to be fellow-citizens with the saints, was such a mystery to the apostles themselves and such a surprise that it concerns us carefully to observe all the circumstances of the beginning of this great work — Christ preached to the Gentiles and believed on in the world. He allows that some Gentiles may before now have stepped into a synagogue, but treats what follows as the deliberate opening of the door.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson set the scene and dispute the man’s standing. Barnes opens with the significance of the chapter, since until now the apostles had preached to the Jews only and had kept their nation’s conviction that salvation was not to be offered beyond it, whereas the whole tendency of the Christian religion was to enlarge and liberalise the mind; he denies that the terms ‘devout’ and ‘one that feared God’ prove Cornelius a Jew or a proselyte, holding there may have been a few Gentiles who feared God and maintained his worship by the light they had; he fixes the ninth hour at three in the afternoon, the usual hour of evening worship; and he argues that ‘Lord’ should have been rendered ‘Sir’, since nothing shows this to be an address to God, the words being what a startled man would naturally say. Ellicott suggests Luke may have had the details from Philip the Evangelist at Caesarea or from Cornelius himself, and holds that this admission became, through its supernatural accompaniments, the ruling case on the reception of Gentiles; he notes that the word for devout is not the one Luke uses elsewhere but marks the devotion proper to Gentile converts to Judaism, finds special significance in the household being included, takes the adverb ‘evidently’ as distinguishing this from a dream or a trance, and observes that Cornelius had accepted the Jewish hours of prayer, the Law serving him too as a schoolmaster bringing him to Christ. Robertson observes that the great Cornelian family of Rome may have had a freedman or descendant here, that Roman centurions always appear favourably in the New Testament, and that Furneaux marks the contrasts between old Joppa and Herod’s Caesarea and between the Galilean fisherman lodging with a tanner and the Roman officer in the seat of government; he takes the two descriptive phrases together as Luke’s standing term for a God-fearing proselyte who had entered synagogue worship without circumcision, and notes the participle is ingressive, so that Cornelius saw the angel come rather than coming.

Clarke and Wesley supply etymology and geography. Clarke derives ‘devout’ from the words for well and worship, making it one who worships the true God and is no idolater, and takes the fear of God as being acquainted with him through his word and laws and not daring to offend one’s Maker and Judge; he notes that Cornelius instructed his family and established the worship of God in his house; and he insists the text is as plain as it can be that an angel really appeared, the manifestation being made openly and at an hour — about three in the afternoon, the time of public prayer — which precluded his being asleep. Wesley calls Cornelius the first fruits of the Gentiles, observes that Philip had already been at Caesarea so that salvation by faith in Jesus was not unknown there, and draws a pattern from the cities: Caesarea was the seat of the civil government as Jerusalem was of the ecclesiastical, and the gospel made its way first through the metropolitan cities — Jerusalem and Caesarea, then Philippi, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus and Rome itself. He adds that the alms were given to the Jews, many of whom were at that time extremely poor, and that the vision was not a trance like Peter’s but plain enough to leave one unaccustomed to such things no room to suspect imposition.

Chrysostom fastens on the rank of the two converts and refuses the obvious inference. Cornelius is not a Jew nor under the Law, but had already forestalled the Christian manner of life; and thus far two persons of high rank have received the faith, the eunuch at Gaza and this man, with great pains taken over both. But it must not be imagined that this was on account of their rank — God forbid — it was on account of their piety; and the reason scripture mentions their dignified stations at all is to show the greatness of that piety, since it is the more wonderful when a man in a position of wealth and power is such as this.

debates: Whether Cornelius was already a proselyte. Barnes denies that the language proves it, and allows for Gentiles who feared God by the light they had; Robertson takes the same two phrases as Luke’s standing description of a God-fearing proselyte outside circumcision; Ellicott finds the word for devout reserved by Luke for Gentile converts to Judaism; Gill says only that he had forsaken Roman idolatry, and Chrysostom that he was neither a Jew nor under the Law.

How the vision is protected against the charge of illusion. Gill, Wesley and Clarke all argue from the waking state and the daylight hour; Calvin makes the recorded hour a deliberate precaution against suspicion of juggling; Ellicott argues from the adverb, which distinguishes this from a dream or a trance.

How ‘Lord’ should be rendered. Barnes alone raises it, arguing for ‘Sir’ on the ground that nothing indicates Cornelius took the figure before him for God, and that the words are simply those of a man startled by an unexpected appearance.

Why the episode is recorded at such length. Henry treats it as a mystery whose every circumstance must be observed; Barnes as the hinge on which the offer of the gospel turns outward; Ellicott as the ruling case for all later admissions of Gentiles.
outliers: Chrysostom alone addresses the social rank of the converts directly, and does so to deny that it had anything to do with God’s dealing with them, treating the mention of their stations as a measure of their piety rather than of their importance.
Wesley alone draws a strategic pattern from the cities, arguing that the gospel advanced first through the metropolitan centres of civil and religious government.
themes: a devout man that feared God
an angel seen in clear daylight
the gospel turning toward the Gentiles
prayers as a memorial before God

5.pericope_label: And now send men to Joppa, and call for one Simon, whose surname is Peter: He lodgeth with one Simon a tanner, whose house is by the sea side: he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do. And when the angel which spake unto Cornelius was departed, he called two of his household servants, and a devout soldier of them that waited on him continually; And when he had declared all these things unto them, he sent them to Joppa.

schools.summary: Calvin and Gill both dwell on the readiness of the obedience. Calvin observes that God dealt most favourably with Cornelius in not requiring him to travel but only to send, so that he stayed at home while Peter endured the journey for his sake; and he denies there is anything strange in such courtesy, since God thrusts the ministers of his word daily upon the unwilling and appears of his own accord to those who do not seek him. He raises the obvious objection — why the angel did not simply teach the man himself — and turns the promptness of the response into a lesson: Cornelius made no delay and did with all diligence what he was told, because he believed the promise, whereas want of faith is precisely why we are slow to follow God; angels do not come flying from heaven to name particular men for us, but the voice of Christ sounds in every ear, bidding us seek and knock. Gill notes that Joppa lay near Caesarea, supposes Simon the tanner was very probably a good man who lodged strangers, observes that Cornelius showed himself ready to obey the moment the angel withdrew, and explains that he told the messengers everything both to send them the more cheerfully and so that they might give Peter a distinct account and move him to come.

Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott supply the setting and the words. Barnes explains that tanneries are erected on the margin of streams or of any body of water so as to carry away the filth produced in dressing skins, Joppa being a seaport on the Mediterranean; and he treats the devout soldier as an instance of the effect of piety in a military officer, since few men have more influence and the effect here is seen in the centurion’s household and in his attendant alike — such men being usually supposed far from the influence of religion, though this shows the labours and disadvantages of a camp are not necessarily hostile to it. He also repeats, with attribution to Clarke, the observation about Jonah and Joppa. Robertson notes that the verb for fetching Peter is middle, of sending another on one’s own account, and occurs only in Acts in the New Testament; that the verb for lodging comes from the word for a stranger received as a guest and can also mean to surprise by strange acts; and that the house stood outside the city walls because of the trade and its need of water, some tanneries standing by the shore at Jaffa still. Ellicott holds that the word describing the soldier implies he was, like his superior officer, a convert to the faith of Israel without being a proselyte in the full sense, and infers the same of the two servants to whom their master told a vision that men living as heathens would have found strange and unintelligible; he treats all such details as light on the character of Cornelius, who so far as his power went sought to lead those under his influence to the truth he had found.

Clarke reads the passage for what it shows about the centurion’s mind and his household. The promise that Peter would tell him what he ought to do implies that matters of great moment had been occupying him: he was satisfied neither with the state of his own soul nor with the religious knowledge he possessed, and had set apart a particular time for extraordinary fasting and prayer that God might reveal more of his will — perhaps having heard of Jesus and been perplexed by the conflicting opinions about him. On the soldier he infers that Cornelius had been attentive to the spiritual interests of his regiment as well as of his family, and remarks that it was not then held a disgrace even among the Romans for a military officer to teach his men lessons of morality and piety toward God, whatever it may be in some Christian countries at present. He also makes the observation about the two missions from Joppa, Jonah’s to the Gentiles of Nineveh and Peter’s to the Gentiles of Caesarea. Wesley takes the same detail in the opposite direction, as a rebuke of his own age rather than a commendation of antiquity: how many such attendants, he asks, have our modern officers? A devout soldier would now be looked upon as little better than a deserter from his colours.

debates: Why the angel does not teach Cornelius directly. Calvin raises the question expressly and treats the sending for Peter as God’s deliberate arrangement, the ordinary ministry being the means through which men are taught; none of the other witnesses on this passage raises it.

What the description of the soldier proves. Ellicott takes the word as marking him a convert to the faith of Israel short of full proselyte status, and extends the inference to the two servants; Barnes and Clarke read it instead as evidence of the centurion’s influence over those under him, Clarke extending it to the whole regiment.

Why the tanner’s house is by the sea. Barnes and Robertson agree it is the requirement of the trade, Robertson adding that this also placed it outside the walls; Gill passes over the location and comments instead on the tanner’s character.
outliers: Wesley alone turns the passage into a complaint about the present, contrasting the centurion’s devout attendant with the officers of his own day and observing that such a soldier would now be reckoned little better than a deserter.

Clarke alone reconstructs an inner history for Cornelius before the vision — dissatisfaction, a set time of fasting and prayer, and perplexity over reports of Jesus — where the others take the narrative as it stands.

Barnes and Clarke both note the coincidence of Joppa as the point of departure for Jonah and for Peter, and Barnes credits Clarke by name for it; it is an observation about the place rather than the text.
themes: Simon the tanner by the sea
he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do
a household led toward the truth
Jonah and Peter sent from Joppa

9.pericope_label: On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour: And he became very hungry, and would have eaten: but while they made ready, he fell into a trance, And saw heaven opened, and a certain vessel descending unto him, as it had been a great sheet knit at the four corners, and let down to the earth: Wherein were all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin are both careful about what was and was not literally seen. Gill measures the road, putting Joppa thirty-six miles from Caesarea and checking that against Josephus, who gives a hundred and fifty furlongs to Antipatris and twenty-six miles thence, unless a nearer way ran along the shore; he explains the hunger by the hour, those being reckoned most religious who ate nothing before the afternoon prayer; and he denies that the heaven was opened literally, as at Christ’s baptism and the stoning of Stephen, taking it as a visionary opening and an emblem of the revealing of the mystery of the calling of the Gentiles, which in other ages was not made known. Calvin sets the two visions side by side and infers that the whole matter was governed by the wonderful counsel of God, who makes Cornelius apt to be taught and kindles in him a desire to learn while making Peter willing to undertake the teaching. On the trance he argues that because our minds are wholly set upon the earth it was fitting that Peter’s should be moved from its place and carried up, and so prepared to receive the oracle; and he distinguishes this opening of heaven from the one in the seventh chapter, where Stephen saw the glory of Christ, whereas Peter saw the visible heaven divided so that a sheet might come from it.

Henry identifies the obstacle the vision exists to remove. Cornelius has had positive orders from heaven to send for Peter, whom otherwise he would not have heard of or heeded; but a second difficulty stands in the way of bringing the two together, namely whether Peter will come when he is sent for. Henry is careful to say what the difficulty is not: not that Peter thought it beneath him to come at another man’s call, nor that he was afraid to preach his doctrine to a person of Cornelius’s standing. It sticks instead at a point of conscience, Cornelius being a worthy man with many good qualities and yet outside the covenant as Peter then understood it.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply distances, customs and grammar. Barnes describes the upper room or roof as the usual place of retirement and prayer, notes that the Jews had two stated seasons of prayer but that the more pious frequently added a third about noon, citing David’s evening, morning and noon and Daniel’s three times a day, and gives the two customary meals as about ten or eleven in the morning and six or seven in the afternoon; on the vision he insists the language is figurative, the opening of heaven deriving from a Hebrew way of speaking as though the sky were a solid expanse that could be opened, and he marks the phrase ‘as it had been’ as important, since the writer does not claim Peter literally saw such an object but gives an imperfect description. Ellicott makes the distance about thirty Roman miles, finds Peter again keeping the Jewish hours of prayer, infers from the hunger that he had taken no food and that this was probably one of the two weekly fast days, notes that the flat eastern housetop was commonly used for prayer, identifies the trance by its technical name and allows that it might in part follow naturally from prolonged fasting, intense prayer and the noonday sun; and he suggests the vision’s content answered to Peter’s own prayer, since a man looking from Joppa across the Great Sea toward the Isles of the Gentiles might well ask by what process their inhabitants were to be brought into the fold. Robertson lays out the four days of the journey, notes the housetop word occurs only here in Acts, that the word for hungry is found nowhere else and probably means very hungry, that the verb for desiring is imperfect and means longing to eat, and that Peter may even have smelt the dishes being prepared — quoting Furneaux that the natural and the supernatural border closely on one another with no definable limits; he also marks the vivid historical present, the perfect participle of a heaven standing open, and the old word for linen cloth found only here.

Clarke and Wesley both relate the vision to the visionary’s condition. Clarke reckons the distance at twelve or fifteen leagues and follows Calmet in calculating that the messengers must have travelled part of the night to arrive toward noon; he explains the party as two household servants sent out of respect to Peter and a soldier probably for their defence, since the roads in Judea were by no means safe; and he sets the meal in its customary place, the ancients having no breakfast and only a slight dinner, with supper the principal meal, and in very ancient times only one meal a day. On the opened heaven he takes the opposite line from the others, treating it as genuine perception: Peter’s mind, entirely spiritualized and absorbed in heavenly contemplation, was capable of discoveries of a spiritual world which with its plenitude of inhabitants surrounds us at all times, though we cannot see it through the dense medium of flesh and blood and their earthly passions. Wesley states the principle the others illustrate, that the symbols in visions and trances are generally suited to the state of the natural faculties.

debates: How far Joppa was from Caesarea. Gill says thirty-six miles and cross-checks Josephus; Ellicott about thirty Roman miles; Robertson twenty-eight; Clarke twelve or fifteen leagues. None of them reconciles the figures, and Clarke builds a timetable on his.

Whether the vision was seen or only represented. Barnes insists the language is figurative and that ‘as it had been’ marks an imperfect description rather than a literal sight; Gill and Calvin both distinguish this opening of heaven from the literal ones granted at Christ’s baptism and to Stephen; Clarke alone treats it as real perception of a spiritual world ordinarily hidden by flesh and blood.

How much of the trance was natural. Ellicott allows that fasting, intense prayer and the noonday sun may in part account for it; Robertson quotes the judgment that the natural and supernatural border on one another without definable limits; Wesley makes it a general rule that the symbols suit the state of the faculties; Calvin instead treats the carrying up of the mind as a necessary preparation, since our minds are otherwise set wholly on the earth.
outliers: Henry alone reads the passage backwards from the difficulty it solves, treating the question as whether Peter will consent to come rather than what Peter saw, and taking pains to acquit him of both pride and cowardice before naming conscience as the obstacle.
Ellicott alone proposes that the vision answered a question Peter had himself been praying about, inferred from the view of the sea toward the Gentile isles.
themes: the journey from Caesarea to Joppa
prayer on the housetop at the sixth hour
hunger and the hour of the meal
symbols suited to the natural faculties
the calling of the Gentiles foreshadowed

13.pericope_label: And there came a voice to him, Rise, Peter; kill, and eat. But Peter said, Not so, Lord; for I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean. And the voice spake unto him again the second time, What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common. This was done thrice: and the vessel was received up again into heaven.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin work on the source of the voice and the reach of the sentence. Gill takes the voice to be formed by an angel or rather by Christ himself, states Peter’s refusal in the first person as a thing contrary to the law of God and to his own practice through his whole life, and explains the threefold repetition without allegory — either the voice spoke three times, or the sheet was let down three times, or both — denying that anything mystical attaches to the number and holding that the purpose was Peter’s firmer assurance of what was shown him. Calvin observes that the voice came from heaven as the sheet did, so that Peter might know both were from God, since the sight would have profited him nothing unless God had by the voice made clean what was unclean before. He expressly declines the allegorical reading some draw from the word ‘kill’ — that men are sacrificed to God by the spiritual sword of the gospel — preferring plainness: God abolishes the law concerning the choice of beasts in order to teach that he rejects no people. On the refusal he notes that Peter objects to God the law God himself made, afraid for good cause to touch what it forbade, and that seeing a show of repugnancy between law and vision he is not hasty but wants his doubt dissolved first. On the answer he extends the sentence past meats to all parts of life: it is not for us to allow or condemn anything, and a mortal man who sets up a new distinction and forbids what God has cleansed takes to himself the authority of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the law, the character and the grammar. Barnes sets out the plea in full: the distinction between clean and unclean animals stood in the Old Testament, the law remained in the Scriptures unrepealed, and Peter, never having violated it, did not dare act against it, there being an apparent variation between that law and this command. On the answer he suspects Peter would have taken the vision to mean only that the distinction in food was to be abolished, whereas the outcome showed a higher design, that those whom the Jews esteemed unclean or profane were no longer to be so reckoned. Ellicott reads the command as confirming the natural promptings of appetite by a divine voice, with a hesitating conscience still in bondage to a ceremonial and transitory law resisting both; he finds the emphatic resistance to a heavenly voice strikingly in harmony with Peter’s character in the Gospels, comparing ‘Be it far from thee, Lord’ and ‘Thou shalt never wash my feet’, and notes that Peter had been taught that what enters the mouth cannot defile without having taken that truth in its fulness; on the answer he presses that clean and unclean came down in the same sheet and reads the interpretation christologically, all that belongs to humanity having been taken up into heaven when the Eternal Word assumed man’s nature and when that nature was raised in the Ascension. Robertson insists the negative is neither a blunt refusal nor merely a mild protest, as Page and Furneaux argue, but a polite refusal with a reason attached, Peter recognising the invitation as the Lord’s and yet declining three times; and on the answer he marks the emphatic position of the pronoun, the idiom meaning ‘do thou stop making common’ what God cleansed, since Peter had just called common what God had invited him to eat.

Clarke and Wesley take up the verb and the hesitation. Clarke argues that the Greek word properly means to slay for sacrifice rather than simply to kill, and draws out the consequence: animals offered in sacrifice were given to God, and when he had received the life the flesh was returned to the offerers to eat, so that every sacrifice carried the nature of a covenant, covenants being made by eating together. He defines the two terms of Peter’s answer, ‘common’ as whatever was in general use among the Gentiles and ‘unclean’ as whatever the Mosaic law forbade, and records that the rabbins themselves and many of the primitive fathers held that the unclean animals of the law signified the Gentiles. On the answer he argues from the right of the lawgiver: he who made the distinction between Jew and Gentile for wise purposes may remove it when and how he pleases, and he who had authority for the first has authority for the last. Wesley turns Peter’s hesitation into a rule with a benefit attached: when God commands a strange or seemingly improper thing the first objection frequently finds pardon, though it ought not to be repeated; and this particular doubt and delay had good effects, since God’s will in so important a point was made the more evident and incontestable, and Peter, having been so slow of belief himself, could the more easily bear the doubting of his brethren afterwards. On the answer he states the argument at its shortest, that nothing but what is clean can come down from heaven.

debates: What the command to ‘kill’ means. Clarke takes the verb in its sacrificial sense and develops a covenant meal from it; Calvin explicitly refuses the allegorical readings drawn from the same word and insists on the plain sense, that the law of clean and unclean beasts is being abolished so as to teach that no people is rejected.

What kind of refusal Peter makes. Robertson distinguishes it from both a blunt refusal and a mild protest, calling it a polite refusal with a reason; Calvin makes it an appeal to God’s own law and a request for the difficulty to be resolved; Barnes makes it obedience to an unrepealed statute; Wesley makes it a pardonable first objection that should not have been repeated.

How far the answer reaches. Barnes takes the food law as the surface and the Gentiles as the real object; Clarke argues from the lawgiver’s right to revoke what he established; Calvin extends the principle to every part of life and turns it against anyone who imposes new distinctions; Ellicott finds the ground of the cleansing in the Incarnation and Ascension.
Whether the threefold repetition signifies anything. Gill denies any mystical meaning in the number and refers it to Peter’s assurance; Robertson simply notes that the refusal was made three times.
outliers: Wesley alone treats Peter’s slowness as providentially useful, arguing that it made the divine will more incontestable and fitted him to be patient with his brethren’s later doubts.
Calvin alone turns the verse into a warning against human legislators, holding that whoever forbids what God has declared clean usurps the authority of God himself.
themes: the law of clean and unclean beasts
Peter’s hesitation before a heavenly voice
the distinction between Jew and Gentile removed

17.pericope_label: Now while Peter doubted in himself what this vision which he had seen should mean, behold, the men which were sent from Cornelius had made enquiry for Simon’s house, and stood before the gate, And called, and asked whether Simon, which was surnamed Peter, were lodged there. While Peter thought on the vision, the Spirit said unto him, Behold, three men seek thee. Arise therefore, and get thee down, and go with them, doubting nothing: for I have sent them. Then Peter went down to the men which were sent unto him from Cornelius; and said, Behold, I am he whom ye seek: what is the cause wherefore ye are come? And they said, Cornelius the centurion, a just man, and one that feareth God, and of good report among all the nation of the Jews, was warned from God by an holy angel to send for thee into his house, and to hear words of thee.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin attend to the text and to the slowness of understanding. Gill notes that Peter had not at once a full knowledge of the matter for all he had heard and seen, and records that Beza’s most ancient copy reads as though the doubting began when he came to himself, having been before as it were out of himself in the trance; he observes that the vision greatly occupied his thoughts, and that the messengers called to the people of the house and asked in a civil and courteous manner. Calvin makes Peter’s delay a mirror of our own: he was taught not only by the vision but by the word of God, and yet in seeing he saw not until the Spirit became his interpreter — and we are far unlike him, being so far from understanding what God wills that many interpretations scarcely suffice us. On the command he shows that scripture uses the phrase about doubting to express what sort the obedience of faith ought to be, citing Paul’s commendation of Abraham for not doubting when God promised him seed though he was aged and past hope of children, and his condemnation of doubting consciences in the matter of meats.

Henry sets the meeting in the wider plan of the mission. Though Paul was designed to be the apostle of the Gentiles and to gather in the harvest among them, and Peter to be the apostle of the circumcision, it is ordered that Peter shall break the ice and reap the first-fruits of the Gentiles; and Henry gives the reason, that the believing Jews, who retained too much of the old leaven of ill-will toward the Gentiles, might be the better reconciled to their admission into the church when it was Peter who first admitted them.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson divide providence, psychology and grammar. Barnes calls the convergence an admirable arrangement of the events of Providence to fit each other, every part of the transaction harmonising with every other and so ordered that just when Peter’s mind was filled with perplexity the very event occurred which relieved it — a coincidence he says is not uncommon in the divine government. Ellicott states the doubt precisely: it might well be asked whether the vision’s teaching went beyond its immediate scope, since Peter could grant that it abrogated the distinction of clean and unclean meats and still hesitate over whether it did more; on the voice he suggests a state of consciousness intermediate between the trance now past and ordinary waking life, the voice no longer coming from heaven to the outward ear but heard as not less divine in the secret recesses of the soul; and he reads the command as addressed to the disciple’s own questionings, so that for a time he was to walk as if blindfold, trusting the hand that guided him, not knowing yet what his Lord was doing but to know hereafter, while he and the messengers alike acted on the promptings of the same Spirit. Robertson takes the verb for perplexity as an intensive compound meaning to be completely at a loss which road to take, found in the New Testament only in Luke and Acts, and observes that Peter was more puzzled out of the ecstasy than in it; notes that the verb for his thinking occurs nowhere else and pictures him revolving the vision through and through; that the messengers called in a loud voice so those inside might hear and kept on inquiring; and that the aorist imperative bids him get down at once while the present bids him go on, the phrase for doubting nothing being a compound denoting a divided mind.

Clarke and Wesley both draw a general lesson from the convergence. Clarke displays the symmetry of the economy of Providence: Cornelius prays and receives a vision preparing him to take instruction from Peter, while Peter prays and receives a vision preparing and disposing him to give instruction to Cornelius; and while Peter is still in doubt and perplexity what the vision fully meant, the messengers, despatched under a special Providence, arrive at the door. Wesley states the same as a maxim, that the things which befall us within and from without at the same time are frequently a key to each other and that such concurrences ought to be diligently attended to; and on the Spirit’s command he marks the gradualness of the preparation, observing how step by step Peter was made ready for this new admonition, and that God is wont to lead his children on by degrees, always giving them light for the present hour.

Cyril of Jerusalem treats the episode as an illustration of the Spirit’s power working in the apostle rather than as a passage to be expounded. He places it in a short series of Peter’s acts — the healing of Aeneas the paralytic in the name of Christ at Lydda, and the raising of Tabitha, rich in good works, at Joppa — and then describes this vision: being on the housetop in a trance he saw heaven opened, and by means of the vessel let down like a sheet full of beasts of every shape and sort he learnt plainly what had not been plain to him before.

debates: What Peter was actually in doubt about. Ellicott defines it as whether the vision reached beyond the food laws; Gill as a want of full knowledge following the trance; Robertson as complete uncertainty which way to turn, made worse rather than better by coming out of the ecstasy; Calvin as the ordinary slowness of even a taught mind until the Spirit interprets.

How the voice at verse 19 differs from the voice in the vision. Ellicott places it in a state between trance and waking, heard inwardly rather than from heaven; the other witnesses pass over the distinction.

What the convergence of the two parties shows. Barnes and Clarke both read it as designed providential arrangement, Clarke laying the two visions side by side as complementary preparations; Wesley turns it into a rule for reading one’s own circumstances; Henry reads it as strategy in the mission, Peter breaking the ice so that Jewish believers would accept what followed.

What ‘doubting nothing’ requires. Robertson glosses it as the absence of a divided mind; Calvin makes it the standing scriptural term for the obedience of faith and supports it from Abraham and from Romans.
outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem alone treats the chapter as evidence in an argument about the Holy Spirit, listing this vision among Peter’s Spirit-empowered acts rather than commenting on the narrative itself.
Wesley alone converts the coincidence of inward and outward events into a general method of discernment, advising that concurrences of this kind be watched for and attended to.
themes: Peter breaking the ice for the Gentiles
Cornelius reported as a just man

23.pericope_label: Then called he them in, and lodged them. And on the morrow Peter went away with them, and certain brethren from Joppa accompanied him. And the morrow after they entered into Cesarea. And Cornelius waited for them, and had called together his kinsmen and near friends. And as Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man. And as he talked with him, he went in, and found many that were come together. And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean. Therefore came I unto you without gainsaying, as soon as I was sent for: I ask therefore for what intent ye have sent for me?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin follow the movement of the narrative and the temper it requires. Gill has Peter take the messengers into Simon’s house with his host’s leave, set provisions before them and lodge them; reckons the last stage of the journey at one day and part of another; observes that the entering in question is into the house and not into the city; describes Peter lifting Cornelius up and setting him on his legs; notes that the company addressed was chiefly if not altogether Gentile; and takes the coming without gainsaying as coming readily and cheerfully, without objecting or making any excuse to put it off. Calvin makes Peter’s promptness the lesson, since being overcome with the authority of God he deliberates no longer, and so we must meekly submit ourselves, nothing remaining once we know God’s will but to run speedily where he calls. He puts the question about the prostration formally — whether Peter refused it only for modesty’s sake or disallowed it as altogether unlawful — and infers from the reason Peter gives that something divine was being offered in it. On the opening of the address he faces its harshness, granting that to tell men they are reckoned so unclean that familiarity with them pollutes the saints might exasperate rather than win them, but explaining that Peter had to speak so lest they suspect him of an evil conscience for coming against the custom delivered by the fathers; and on the last verse he calls the readiness the holy silence of faith, receiving meekly what God commands and driving far away all contrary reasons that intrude themselves.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle chronology, custom and grammar. Barnes lays out the four days that pass before the meeting, identifies the brethren as six from the parallel in the eleventh chapter, treats the prostration as profound civil regard rather than religious homage since it was usual in Oriental countries to prostrate oneself before men of rank, and takes Peter’s refusal with Doddridge as a disclaimer of anything beyond the respect due in civil life; on the rule about Gentiles he holds it was not explicitly enjoined by Moses but seemed implied, the design being to keep Israel separate by forbidding alliances with idolatrous nations, a command the Jews afterwards perverted into a ban on intercourse of every kind. Ellicott places the arrival of the messengers in the afternoon, grounds the number of witnesses in the requirement that every word be established in the mouth of two or three, supposes the kinsmen and friends to have been in sympathy with Cornelius already, calls the prostration the extremest form of Eastern homage and compares Jairus before Jesus and John before the angel, and reads Peter’s refusal as treating it as homage due to God alone — contrasting that sharply with the ceremonial of those who claim to be his successors; on the rule he says Peter speaks from the standpoint of traditional Pharisaism rather than of the Law itself, and describes the practice, the strict Jew refusing to enter a Gentile’s house, share a couch, or eat from the same vessel, the very dust of a heathen city being defiling. Robertson notes the active voice in the lodging, the periphrastic imperfect of eager expectation in the waiting, the rare use of a word for blood relations, and a construction at the entrance that most commentators consider inexplicable; on the rule he states plainly that no Old Testament regulation forbids such social contact, the rabbis having added it and made it binding by custom, and remarks that nothing is more binding on the average person than social custom; and he glosses the phrase about gainsaying as without answering back, since Peter had now stepped over the line of Jewish custom.

Clarke and Wesley supply detail and polemic. Clarke observes that the messengers had walked a long journey in a short time and needed refreshment; that the six brethren were necessary because on no slight evidence would even converted Jews accept what was coming; that the Syriac distinguishes kinsmen, domestics and friends, so that Cornelius had gathered the whole circle of his intimate acquaintance; and that Cornelius, whose visitor had been announced by an angel, may have supposed Peter himself an angel of a superior order and prostrated himself accordingly, offering the highest act of civil respect. He marks the turning point plainly: Peter now begins to understand the vision, a Gentile is not to be avoided because he is a Gentile, and God is taking down the partition wall. Wesley notes that Cornelius engaged in no secular business during that solemn time but was altogether intent on this one thing; states Peter’s refusal at its bluntest, that he is a man and not God, who alone ought to be worshipped, and asks whether all his pretended successors have attended to this; observes that Peter speaks sparingly of his own former doubt and his late vision; and explains the closing question as put not for Peter’s information but so that the rest might be informed and Cornelius himself the more impressed by telling the story.

Chrysostom attends to the manners of the scene and to the reason for the companions. It is good, he says, that Peter first gives the messengers friendly treatment after the fatigue of their journey and makes them at home with him, and only on the following day sets out. He reads the presence of the brethren from Joppa as Providence ordering matters in advance, since they would afterwards be needed as witnesses when Peter had to justify what he had done; and he notes that Cornelius, on his side, was waiting and had called together his kinsmen and near friends.

debates: What kind of homage Cornelius offered. Barnes and Clarke both keep it civil, Clarke suggesting Cornelius may have taken Peter for an angel; Ellicott and Calvin both find something more in it, Calvin inferring from Peter’s stated reason that the worship had a divine character, Ellicott that Peter treated it as due to God alone. Barnes and Calvin thus reach opposite conclusions from the same refusal.

Whether the ban on Gentile company was law or custom. Robertson denies any Old Testament regulation and assigns it to the rabbis; Ellicott assigns it to traditional Pharisaism rather than the Law; Barnes allows that it was not explicitly enjoined but was implied in institutions meant to keep Israel separate, and that the Jews then perverted it.

Why Peter opens with so unwelcome a statement. Calvin treats it as necessary self-defence, lest the hearers think him a despiser of the law acting against conscience; Clarke reads the same words as the moment Peter grasps his own vision.

Why Peter asks a question he has already been answered. Clarke and Wesley agree that the point is the company rather than Peter, so that all present may hear the account and Cornelius be the more impressed in giving it; Barnes prefers that Peter wanted the fuller reasons from Cornelius’s own lips.
outliers: Ellicott and Wesley both turn Peter’s refusal of homage into an argument against papal claims — Ellicott contrasting the ceremonial of those who claim to be his successors, Wesley asking whether the pretended successors have attended to the verse. No other witness on this passage raises the question.
Chrysostom alone comments on the courtesy of the arrangements — feeding and lodging the tired messengers before setting out — treating the delay as a virtue rather than as a detail of the itinerary.
themes: four days from vision to meeting
I myself also am a man
calling no man common or unclean

30.pericope_label: And Cornelius said, Four days ago I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour I prayed in my house, and, behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing, And said, Cornelius, thy prayer is heard, and thine alms are had in remembrance in the sight of God. Send therefore to Joppa, and call hither Simon, whose surname is Peter; he is lodged in the house of one Simon a tanner by the sea side: who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee. Immediately therefore I sent to thee; and thou hast well done that thou art come. Now therefore are we all here present before God, to hear all things that are commanded thee of God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin attend to the manner of the speech. Gill notes the Syriac addition and describes Cornelius as speaking in a very submissive and humble manner; takes the prayer that was heard as the one he was then particularly making, together with others offered before; and finds in the promptness of the sending a disclaimer of pride, vanity and imperiousness, since Cornelius did not send of his own motion but by divine order, which he executed the very same hour. Calvin holds that the speech is otherwise only a bare repetition of the history, whose sum is that Cornelius called Peter at God’s commandment. On the disputed word he observes that the old interpreter omitted ‘fasting’ and judges this to have been done through error or negligence, since it stands in all the Greek books; and he explains that Cornelius mentions the fast partly so that we may know he did not pray coldly or perfunctorily at that time. On the closing sentence he explains why it is said at all, since a teacher is much moved to take pains when he is confident his hearers will profit by it, and leaves open whether the words are an oath or simply a profession that the company was gathered as in the sight of God.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson work the chronology and the idiom. Barnes fixes the hour at three in the afternoon and notes that the figure described as an angel in the earlier narrative is here called a man, since that was his appearance. Ellicott will not fix the hour of the vision, holding only that it cannot have been much before noon; he argues from the fast-days observed by devout Jews that the vision may have fallen on the second day of the week and Peter’s on the fifth, so that the meeting in the house probably took place on the Sabbath. On the answer to the prayer he observes that the singular here is more definite than the plural used earlier, and infers that what was asked must have been fuller light and knowledge of the truth: a man who had heard of the teaching and life of Jesus, whether through Philip’s work at Caesarea or through the brother-officer once stationed at Capernaum, might well seek guidance about the conditions of admission to the society that acknowledged him. On the closing words he notes that the phrase rendered ‘thou hast well done’ was in social usage an expression of heartfelt gratitude rather than mere approval, and hears in the last sentence both readiness and anxiety, the assembled circle sharing Cornelius’s solicitude and willing to obey whatever came as God’s command while hoping it would not impose a burden too heavy to bear. Robertson reckons the days backwards from the fourth, notes the periphrastic imperfect with an accusative of extent so that Cornelius kept the whole ninth hour of prayer, calls the thanks a regular formula, and remarks that Cornelius commends Peter for his courage in breaking from Jewish custom and takes no offence at the implied superiority of Jew over Gentile.

Clarke and Wesley supply the calendar and the application. Clarke calculates the fast as running from three o’clock on the preceding day to three on this one, and rejects the supposition that Cornelius fasted four days together — adding that even on that view he ate one meal on each day; he records that the word for fasting is wanting in several of the best manuscripts and in the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate. On the prayer he draws a rule about the use of light already given: Cornelius prayed, fasted and gave alms, and it was in this way that he looked for salvation, not to purchase it — a thought which does not appear to have entered his mind — but as the means of bringing his soul to the knowledge of the truth; there was in his case no open vision, he used the light and power God had already given him, and God increased his gifts mightily. He also notes that several versions read ‘before thee’ rather than ‘before God’, and pictures the people waiting for the preacher with every heart filled with expectation. Wesley sets out the four days in order — the vision, the messengers’ arrival at Joppa, Peter’s setting out, the arrival at Caesarea — supposes Cornelius had doubtless been praying for instruction how to worship God in the most acceptable manner, and gives the last sentence its widest application, calling it the language of every truly Christian congregation.

debates: Whether the word ‘fasting’ belongs in the text. Clarke reports it wanting in several of the best manuscripts and in four versions; Calvin, writing much earlier, notes the old interpreter’s omission and attributes it to error or negligence on the ground that the word stands in all the Greek books known to him. The two witnesses reach opposite conclusions from the evidence available to each.

How the four days are counted. Robertson reckons backwards from the fourth day; Wesley assigns an event to each; Clarke uses the phrase to measure the length of the fast rather than the interval; Ellicott uses it to place the meeting on a Sabbath.

What Cornelius had been praying for. Wesley supposes instruction in the most acceptable way of worship; Ellicott argues for fuller light and specifically for the terms of admission to the new society; Gill leaves it as the prayer then being offered; Clarke treats prayer, fasting and alms together as the means by which he sought the knowledge of the truth.

What the closing sentence means. Barnes takes it as implying that the company believed God saw them and were assembled at his command; Ellicott hears anxiety in it as well as readiness; Calvin leaves open whether it is an oath or a simple profession; Clarke notes the variant ‘before thee’.
outliers: Clarke alone turns the passage into a doctrine about the use of light already possessed, insisting that Cornelius did not suppose his devotions purchased anything but used what he had been given, and that God increased his gifts accordingly.
Ellicott alone attempts to date the meeting to a particular day of the week, reasoning from the customary Jewish fast-days to place it on a Sabbath.
themes: sending for Peter at divine order
we are all here present before God

34.pericope_label: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him. The word which God sent unto the children of Israel, preaching peace by Jesus Christ: (he is Lord of all:) That word, I say, ye know, which was published throughout all Judea, and began from Galilee, after the baptism which John preached; How God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Ghost and with power: who went about doing good, and healing all that were oppressed of the devil; for God was with him.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin mark the structure and define the terms. Gill notes that everything before this was only a preface and that the sermon proper now begins, and takes the word sent to the children of Israel as the doctrine of the gospel, which God of his infinite wisdom and rich grace sent first to the Jews by the ministry of the apostles; on the reach of the promise he extends it to any Gentile nation in the Roman empire and even to Scythia or the most uncultivated parts of the universe. Calvin observes that scripture uses the phrase about opening the mouth wherever a grave or weighty oration is meant, as when Jesus opened his mouth to preach to his disciples on the weightiest matters — the sense being that a man began to speak having first well bethought himself what he would say. On the two terms of the promise he holds that they comprehend the integrity of the whole life, the fear of God being nothing else than godliness and religion, and the working of righteousness that equity which men use among themselves, taking heed lest they hurt any man and studying to do good to all; and since the law consists of these two parts, no man proves himself to God who does not refer and direct all his actions to that rule.

Henry treats what stands here as an abstract or summary of the sermon rather than the whole of it, since there is reason to think Peter testified and exhorted with many other words to the same purport. He finds in the opening phrase a mark of manner as well as of form: it intimates that Peter expressed himself with a great deal of solemnity and gravity, and yet with freedom and copiousness.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the principle and limit the inference. Barnes explains respect of persons as showing favour on account of rank, family, wealth or any partiality, as a judge does who favours one party for such a reason, and reads the following verse as the ground of the assertion, the favours of God not being confined to the Jew but extended to all others on the same principle; on the next verse he reports that few passages in the New Testament have perplexed critics more, since it is difficult to say what the accusative refers to, and warns that the English rendering misleads by making it identical with what follows, where a different word stands. Ellicott notes that Peter had already seen in his Master the absence of respect of persons that even his enemies acknowledged and that James presses the same quality within the same limits, while both had still to learn its wider application; and he takes the promise as far-reaching, applying not only to those who know the name of Christ and believe when he is preached but to all who in any age or country fear God according to the measure of their knowledge and work righteousness according to their belief and opportunities. Robertson calls the opening a solemn formula and also good elocution, notes that the verb for perceiving is a middle denoting mental action, and states the conclusion narrowly: a Gentile would not have to become a Jew in order to become a Christian — something Peter had evidently not perceived before, since at Pentecost, speaking of the promise to those afar off, he had understood that they must first become Jews and then Christians, so that this new idea makes a revolution in his outlook.

Clarke and Wesley both take the promise as widely as the words allow. Clarke denies partiality in both directions, that God neither esteems a Jew for being a Jew nor detests a Gentile for being a Gentile, and observes that the contrary was a long and deeply rooted opinion among the Jews — Peter’s own until the vision of this chapter. On the second verse he describes the accepted man by his conduct: in every nation he who according to his light and privileges fears God and worships him alone, works righteousness, abstains from all evil, gives to all their due and injures neither the body, soul nor reputation of his neighbour is accepted with him; it is not the nation, kindred, profession, mode or form of worship that the just God regards, but the character. Wesley reads the first statement as meaning in a particular sense that God does not confine his love to one nation and in a general sense that he is loving to every man and wills all men to be saved; and on the second he defines both terms — reverencing God as great, wise and good, the cause, end and governor of all things, and from that regard not only avoiding known evil but endeavouring by the best light he has to do all things well — and concludes that such a man is accepted through Christ though he does not know him, adding that the assertion is express and admits of no exception.

Cyril of Jerusalem uses these verses as proof texts rather than expounding them. He quotes the words about the word God sent to the children of Israel in support of the lordship of the Son, identifying the Lord of all with him who was born in Bethlehem of Judaea according to the angel’s announcement to the shepherds. On the baptism that John preached he sets herald against King in a series of contrasts: John was great, but what is he to the Lord? His was a loud-sounding voice, but what in comparison with the Word? Very noble was the herald, but what in comparison with the King? Noble was he that baptized with water, but what to him who baptizes otherwise?

debates: How far ‘accepted with him’ reaches. Wesley states that such a man is accepted through Christ though he does not know him, and that the assertion admits of no exception; Clarke likewise makes character rather than nation, profession or form of worship the thing God regards; Ellicott extends it to all ages and countries according to each man’s measure of knowledge. Robertson and Barnes keep the statement to the immediate issue — that a Gentile need not first become a Jew — and draw no conclusion about those who have never heard.

What was new to Peter here. Robertson makes it the discovery that conversion no longer runs through Judaism, and dates Peter’s older view to the Pentecost sermon; Clarke makes it the abandonment of a deeply rooted national opinion; Ellicott holds Peter had long seen the principle in his Master and needed only to learn its extent.

What the two terms of verse 35 mean. Calvin takes them as the two tables of the law, godliness and equity, comprehending the whole of life; Wesley defines them as reverence for God and, arising from it, the endeavour to do all things well; Clarke expands the second into a list of duties owed to a neighbour’s body, soul and reputation.

What the accusative in verse 36 governs. Barnes reports the passage as among the most perplexing in the New Testament and rejects the assumption behind the English rendering; Gill treats the word simply as the doctrine of the gospel sent first to the Jews.
outliers: Cyril of Jerusalem alone takes the verses out of their narrative setting and uses them in doctrinal argument, one to establish the lordship of the Son and the other to subordinate John the Baptist to Christ.

Henry alone comments on the manner of delivery rather than the matter, reading the opening formula as evidence of solemnity joined with freedom, and treating the recorded sermon as a summary of something longer.
themes: God is no respecter of persons
whether a Gentile must first become a Jew
Jesus anointed with the Holy Ghost

39.pericope_label: And we are witnesses of all things which he did both in the land of the Jews, and in Jerusalem; whom they slew and hanged on a tree: Him God raised up the third day, and shewed him openly; Not to all the people, but unto witnesses chosen before of God, even to us, who did eat and drink with him after he rose from the dead. And he commanded us to preach unto the people, and to testify that it is he which was ordained of God to be the Judge of quick and dead. To him give all the prophets witness, that through his name whosoever believeth in him shall receive remission of sins.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin attend to the sense of the witnessing and to the divine restraint. Gill takes the apostles to have been eyewitnesses of Christ’s going from place to place, of the good he did everywhere and of the miracles he wrought; notes that the resurrection, though sometimes ascribed to Christ himself as God, whereby he was declared to be the Son of God, is here as generally ascribed to God the Father; and understands the restriction of the appearances as excluding the Jews who crucified him, observing that not even the whole body of Christians saw him, though five hundred brethren did at one time. Calvin marks a change of sense in the word witness within a few lines: Peter first says that he and his fellows in office saw with their own eyes everything they report of Christ, and then uses the term of an office, saying they were appointed witnesses by God. On the restriction he puts the objection formally — why did God not show his Son openly to all men after the resurrection? — and answers first that even if no reason could be shown, the counsel of God alone ought to suffice sober and modest men, and then that God used this moderation to a good end, the certainty of the resurrection being proved by many and firm testimonies while the restraint served to exercise faith.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the wording and the evidential force. Barnes corrects the English, which seems to describe two acts of slaying and then suspending, whereas the original says simply that they put him to death by suspending him on a tree, the tree being the cross; he reads the showing openly as manifest enough to leave no room for doubt, holds that a general appearance was not necessary to establish the resurrection since Christ showed himself to many, and takes the eating and drinking as furnishing the clearest possible proof that he was truly risen. Ellicott hears in the claim to witness the terms of the commission given at the opening of the book, and argues that ‘the land of the Jews’, spoken at Caesarea by a Galilean, must bear the narrower sense of Judea, which then implies a Judean ministry of which the first three Gospels record very little; he renders the showing literally as giving him to be manifest, prefers ‘appointed’ to ‘chosen before’ and notes that the word occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, and names the three recorded instances of eating and drinking, calling this the crucial test that showed the Form the disciples had looked on was no phantom of the imagination. Robertson observes that Peter appeals both to what his audience know and to what the disciples know, having made the same claim at Pentecost; calls the phrase about being made manifest peculiar and found only here and in a quotation in Romans; describes the word for the chosen witnesses as a double compound meaning designated beforehand by hand, as old as Plato but here alone in the New Testament; and finds in the restriction of the appearances the historian’s candour, since Peter states the thing as it happened rather than strengthening his case by claiming that friends and foes alike had seen the risen Christ.

Clarke and Wesley take the evidential and the practical sides. Clarke suggests the claim to witness may take in not only the twelve but the six brethren Peter had brought with him; explains why the death is stated at all, since the truth of the resurrection depends on the reality of the death and this had to be shown to rest on indubitable evidence; and argues the interval both ways, that Christ lay long enough to prove he was dead and not so long that his disciples could be supposed to have had time to practise some imposture, the tomb being guarded throughout. On the restricted appearances he explains that the public were no longer to be instructed by Christ in person, so that the time after the resurrection was devoted to furnishing those who would preach redemption in his name, God choosing as witnesses the men every way best qualified to attest the fact. Wesley glosses the eating and drinking as conversing familiarly and continually with him, as in the time of his ministry; takes the appointment as Judge of quick and dead to cover all men, whether alive at his coming or dead before it, and reads it as declaring in the strongest terms how entirely the hearers’ happiness depended on a timely and humble subjection to him; and on the last verse notes that Peter, speaking to heathens, quotes no prophet in particular, that the promise runs to everyone who believes whether Jew or Gentile, and that such a man receives remission of sins though he had not before either feared God or worked righteousness.

debates: Why the risen Christ appeared only to chosen witnesses. Barnes says a general appearance was unnecessary; Gill takes the exclusion to fall on those who crucified him; Clarke explains it from the purpose of the interval, which was to furnish the preachers; Calvin declines to require a reason at all before offering one, that the restraint exercised faith; Robertson turns the restriction into evidence of the narrator’s candour.

What the claim to be a witness means. Calvin distinguishes two senses within a few lines, eyewitness and appointed officer; Clarke widens the first to include the six brethren from Joppa; Ellicott ties it to the commission of the first chapter.

How far ‘the land of the Jews’ extends. Ellicott argues for the narrow sense of Judea, and draws from it an implied ministry the Synoptics barely record; Robertson takes it of the whole country including Galilee and Peraea.

Who receives remission. Wesley says everyone who believes, Jew or Gentile, receives it though he had not before feared God or worked righteousness — a qualification that pulls against the reading he gave of the earlier verse in this same sermon, where fearing God and working righteousness were what made a man accepted.
outliers: Robertson alone treats the limitation of the appearances as an argument for the account’s honesty rather than a difficulty to be explained away, on the ground that an inventor would have claimed more.
Clarke alone reasons about the length of the interval in the tomb as a deliberate balance between proving death and precluding fraud, and brings in the guard as part of the argument.
themes: slain and hanged on a tree
shewn openly but not to all
eating and drinking after the resurrection
remission of sins through his name

44.pericope_label: While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word. And they of the circumcision which believed were astonished, as many as came with Peter, because that on the Gentiles also was poured out the gift of the Holy Ghost. For they heard them speak with tongues, and magnify God. Then answered Peter, Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we? And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of the Lord. Then prayed they him to tarry certain days.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin handle the gift and the company’s reaction. Gill takes the tongues for divers languages the speakers had never learned and did not before understand, in which they spoke of the wonderful works of God as the apostles had at Pentecost, speaking greatly in his praise and giving thanks for the grace bestowed on them. Calvin calls the event a new miracle by which God declares the doctrine of the gospel common to Gentiles as well as Jews, and an excellent seal of the calling of the Gentiles, since the Lord would never have bestowed the graces of his Spirit on them except to declare that they too were adopted into the society of the covenant — while noting that these gifts differ from the grace of regeneration. On the astonishment he finds it strange that men who knew Peter had been sent by God should wonder at what followed, and turns the difficulty into an observation about how God regards imperfect faith: Luke calls these men faithful while they were still possessed by a wicked error, since the Lord does not at once wipe away every cloud of ignorance from his own, and such clouds do not darken the praise of faith before God, who pardons the errors and favours the faith as if it were pure and plain.

Henry treats these verses as the issue and effect of the sermon, and says Peter did not labour in vain among them but that they were all brought home to Christ. He notes that God owned Peter’s word by conferring the Holy Ghost on the hearers immediately upon their hearing it, and reads the interruption as a happy one: while Peter was yet speaking, and perhaps designed to say more, he was superseded by visible indications of the Spirit’s presence.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson describe the gift and its reception. Barnes takes the descent as endowing them with the power of speaking in languages other than their own, notes that Peter makes much of this in the argument of the following chapter, and finds in it God’s demonstration that the Gentiles were to be admitted to the same privileges and the same salvation as the Jews; the astonishment he explains simply, that those present were amazed Gentiles should be admitted to the same favour as themselves. Ellicott reads the descent as a sudden thrill of spiritual joy and elevation showing itself, as on the Day of Pentecost, in a burst of unpremeditated praise, the tongues appearing not as instruments of teaching but in magnifying God, and observes that nothing here indicates the utterance was in any language other than those the speakers already knew; he dwells on the astonishment of Peter’s companions as a testimony beyond suspicion to the reality of the gift, since they were plainly not sharers in the joy they were compelled to recognise as the Spirit’s work, listening with amazement as the rapturous chant burst from the lips of heathens not yet baptised, and he calls this one definite fulfilment of Peter’s vision. Robertson notes the genitive absolute showing the speech still in progress and that Peter was plainly interrupted, glosses the word for amazement as standing out of oneself, and puts the weight of the clause on the Spirit being poured out even upon Gentiles.

Clarke and Wesley read the descent as evidence. Clarke doubts that the recorded words are all the apostle spoke, holding rather that the Spirit fell while he continued to discourse, and says the descent was known by the hearers being enabled to speak with different kinds of tongues, though in what manner the gift was bestowed we cannot tell. He explains the astonishment of the Jewish believers from a settled maxim of theirs, that the divine influence could not be revealed to anyone dwelling beyond the precincts of the promised land, and that none of them believed the Spirit could be communicated to a Gentile at all — so that it is no wonder they were amazed to see it given so liberally. On the magnifying of God he remarks that they had got new hearts as well as new tongues, and that having believed with the heart unto righteousness their tongues made confession unto salvation. Wesley calls them consecrated to God as the first fruits of the Gentiles, and takes the whole as a clear and satisfactory evidence that God had accepted them as well as the Jews.

Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem take the two ends of the passage. Chrysostom reads the timing as providential management: God does not suffer the speech to be finished, nor the baptism to take place upon a command of Peter, but waits until it has been made evident how admirable the hearers’ state of mind is, and the work of teaching has begun, and they have believed that baptism is the remission of sins — and then forthwith the Spirit comes upon them, disposed so as to provide Peter with a mighty ground to stand on when he must afterwards defend what he did. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the reason water is still required once the Spirit has come: since man is of twofold nature, soul and body, the purification is twofold also, the water cleansing the body and the Spirit sealing the soul, that we may draw near to God with our heart sprinkled by the Spirit and our body washed with pure water.

debates: What the tongues were. Gill, Barnes and Clarke all take them for languages the speakers had never learned; Ellicott reads the same words as a burst of unpremeditated praise and points out that nothing in the passage says the utterance was in any unfamiliar language. The two readings differ on the plain sense of the verse, not on its application.

Why the Spirit came before the baptism and before the sermon was over. Chrysostom makes the timing deliberate, so that Peter should have unanswerable ground for what he did next; Henry treats the interruption as God owning the word; Robertson simply records that Peter was cut short.

Why Peter’s own companions were astonished. Clarke explains it from the maxim that the divine influence was confined to the holy land; Barnes from their assumption about Gentile standing; Ellicott turns their surprise into evidence of the gift’s reality; Calvin alone finds the astonishment itself hard to account for, given that they knew Peter had been sent by God.
Why water baptism is still required. Cyril of Jerusalem alone answers, arguing from the twofold nature of man that the purification must be twofold, water for the body and the Spirit for the soul.
outliers: Calvin alone uses the episode to make a point about imperfect faith, observing that Luke calls these men faithful while they were still held by a wicked error, and that God pardons such errors rather than letting them darken the praise of faith.
Ellicott alone reads the tongues here as praise in familiar speech rather than in foreign languages, and rests the reading on the silence of the text.
